pages.text: A journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step.

pages.title: The smaller decision
body: It’s late. Your phone is beside you, and you’re making another promise about never watching porn again. You might mean every word.
But at midnight, the useful decision is smaller: what will you do with the phone before you go to sleep?
Put it somewhere you can’t reach from bed. Check the alarm first. If you need to receive urgent calls, keep those available.
A shelf across the room is enough if leaving it outside the bedroom would cause problems. Put the laptop away too. Otherwise, you’ve moved one screen and left another waiting.

pages.title: An earlier moment

steps: Get into bed to answer a message

body: Think of the evening that usually goes wrong. You get into bed to answer a message. Then you check a feed. Twenty minutes later, you’re searching for something you had decided to stop watching.
By then, putting the phone down feels much harder. Charging it elsewhere changes an earlier decision, before that search begins.
This won’t make every urge disappear. It gives you a few seconds in which you have to get up and choose.

Use those seconds to begin something you’ve already decided on: wash, read a few pages, or turn out the light. Another search for recovery advice can wait until tomorrow if it keeps you awake beside the same screen.
Marcus Aurelius reminded himself to deal with the trouble in front of him instead of carrying every possible future trouble into it.
You can apply that idea tonight. You don’t have to settle the coming year before putting the phone down.

pages.title: Where you’re starting
body: Before you finish, write a few facts about where you’re starting. When do you usually watch? How much time does it take, if you know? What does it interrupt? What tends to happen afterwards?
Approximate answers are useful. Guessing precise numbers isn’t. You’ll return to these notes later to see what changed. Tonight, they only need to be honest.

pages.text: Well begun is half done.

pages.title: Prepare for tonight
body: Start one private note called My recovery plan.

Write your porn boundary and what you know about your starting point: when you usually watch, roughly how often or for how long, what it interrupts, and what you do after an urge or slip. Write “unknown” where needed.
Prepare tonight: set the alarm, put the phone out of reach from bed, and put other devices away.
Keep needed calls and accessibility available. If the device must stay close, close the content and choose a practical limit on browsing.
pages.done: Your starting notes are saved and tonight’s device setup is ready.

pages.title: Lesson complete.
pages.body: One thing left today — the task.

pages.text: Begin at once to live, and count each separate day as a separate life.

pages.title: Small conveniences
body: A bookmark saves you a few clicks. So does a familiar account, an open tab, or a folder you know by heart.
Those small conveniences matter when you’re tired and don’t want to think. Today, remove one that repeatedly brings you back to porn.

head: What you use
What to change
rows: Delete it without a last look

body: Start with what you actually use. If it’s a particular account, unfollow or block it. If it’s saved material, delete it without opening each item for a last look.
If the material is already gone, look at what still happens before you watch. Perhaps you keep opening the same feed in bed. Moving the charger may matter more than another hour of deleting files.

pages.title: What surrounds a habit
body: Wendy Wood and her colleagues studied students who moved to another university. Some habits changed when the surroundings changed; others carried over when familiar cues remained.
The study looked at everyday activities, not porn, and students weren’t randomly assigned to move. It suggests a useful place to look: the things around a habit that make it easy to repeat.
For example, clearing your desk won’t help much if the laptop still opens to the same account. Turning off its notifications might.
A blocker can add another obstacle, but check its settings without searching for sexual material. Keep access to work, calls, and anything else you need.

pages.title: Give it an ending
body: Give this job an ending. Twenty minutes is enough for a first pass.
You can spend a whole evening comparing blockers, organising folders, and calling it preparation. Stop when one change is in place. Then use the rest of the evening.
The change should be easy to describe: “I removed that account from my feed,” or “The charger is on the kitchen shelf.” Feeling determined is welcome, but it isn’t the thing you’ll check tomorrow.
Check whether the account stayed out of the feed or the phone stayed out of bed. If the change didn’t help, those details will tell you what to try next.

pages.prompt: What still makes porn easy to reach?
pages.instr: Choose all that fit. Choose F alone if it fits.

options.t: Saved material or bookmarks
A feed or account that leads to porn
A device beside me where I usually watch
An empty hour with nothing planned
Something else
Nothing clear right now

pages.lead: Choose one thing to change today.
body: If nothing stands out, check that your existing device setup still works.

pages.text: First say to yourself what you would be; and then do what you have to do.

pages.title: Remove easy access to porn
body: Spend up to twenty minutes making one change where you usually watch. Clear your own space, remove saved porn or bookmarks without reopening the content, or leave an account used to find it.
If there’s nothing relevant to remove, check yesterday’s device setup and fix any inconvenience. Write the useful change under Access in your plan.
pages.done: You’ve made one useful change, or confirmed that the existing setup works. Stop there rather than browse for more things to delete.

pages.title: Lesson complete.
pages.body: Your answers are saved to the log. One thing left today — the task.

pages.text: An early-morning walk is a blessing for the whole day.

pages.title: Too many decisions
body: You decide to take a walk when you feel the urge. First, you check the weather. Then you choose a podcast, answer a message, and look for your shoes.
Ten minutes later, you’re still sitting with the phone. The walk was a reasonable idea. Starting it involved too many decisions.
Choose a nearby place now. That might be the corner shop, a short walk around the block, or the kitchen where someone else is sitting.
Know what you’ll do when you get there. “Go somewhere else” leaves another choice to make when you’re already struggling.

pages.title: Close it, then move
body: Close the content before you move. Taking the same search into a different room changes very little. Put the phone away, unless you need it for safety or access, and begin the activity you chose.
Make tea, sit with a book, or take the short walk. It can feel dull at first. The point is to stop spending the next ten minutes in the same search.
Check whether this works at the hour you need it. A café that’s open in the afternoon won’t help after midnight. A long walk may be impractical if you’re caring for a child.
In those cases, choose a room nearby. If moving is difficult, put the device farther away and bring a different activity within reach.

pages.title: Try it today
body: Try the steps today while you aren’t struggling with an urge. Find your shoes, check the door, and spend a few minutes in the place you chose.
Fix anything that makes starting awkward. This shows you can follow the steps; you’ll learn whether they help with an urge when one happens.
Decide what you’ll do when you return as well. Coming back to an open laptop can restart the search. Leave it closed and have the next activity ready, whether that’s food, work, or bed.
The walk doesn’t have to solve the whole evening. It should help you start the part that comes after it.

pages.text: All truly great thoughts are conceived while walking.

pages.title: Choose where to go instead
body: Name an exact place you can go when browsing starts: the kitchen table, a shared room, or a safe walk around the block. Try it for ten to twenty minutes today, after closing any triggering content.

If movement is limited, change your seat or put the device away and bring another activity within reach. Keep a phone when needed for safety or access. Save the place and first step under First response.
pages.done: You’ve tried the change and saved the steps. If you can’t try it today, prepare an accessible option and choose when to try it.

pages.title: Lesson complete.
pages.body: One thing left today — the task.

pages.text: There is a time for many words, and there is also a time for sleep.

pages.title: An evening with no ending
body: You finish a long day and want some time that’s yours. One video feels like a fair reward. Then another begins.
Eventually, the evening you wanted has taken the sleep you needed. Tomorrow starts with less energy, and the same bargain becomes tempting again.
Give entertainment an ending before you’re exhausted. A programme has a final episode; a feed usually doesn’t.

Choose when you’ll stop opening new things, where the phone will stay, and what you’ll do afterwards. If work ends late, build around that. Copying someone else’s early bedtime won’t make your shift shorter.

pages.title: Tiredness you stop noticing
body: In a controlled experiment, Hans Van Dongen and colleagues gave healthy adults restricted sleep opportunities over two weeks. Attention worsened across days in the groups allowed four or six hours in bed each night.
Their ratings of sleepiness didn’t fully track the decline. This was a sleep study, not a study of porn. It does show why “I’m used to being tired” deserves a second look.
An early alarm isn’t a repair for a very late night. Choose a wake time that leaves enough time for sleep.
If work or caring duties keep making that impossible, the problem may need practical help beyond a bedtime rule.

pages.title: After the phone goes away
body: Plan for being awake after the phone goes away. Leave a book nearby or choose something quiet you can listen to without opening a feed.
You can make sleep easier to start, but you can’t force yourself to fall asleep at a particular minute. Lying awake doesn’t cancel the work you did to end the browsing.
For the next few nights, notice what you can check: when browsing ended, where the phone stayed, and whether your schedule allowed time for sleep. On Day 7, you’ll look back at those details.
If the stopping time was unrealistic, change it. If sleep remains persistently difficult, seek qualified help rather than adding stricter alarms. Tonight’s job is to give sleep a fair chance.

pages.text: Sleep that knits up the ravelled sleave of care.

pages.title: Prepare for sleep
body: Plan the next sleep period. Choose a realistic wake time, when browsing ends, where the device goes, and a quiet activity before bed. Allow enough sleep for your circumstances.
If you can’t sleep, avoid restarting the feed in bed. Save the steps under Night routine and set a Day 7 reminder to check what happened.
pages.done: The sleep plan and device setup are ready. Falling asleep on command isn’t part of the task.

pages.title: Lesson complete.
pages.body: One thing left today — the task.

pages.text: No great thing is created suddenly.

pages.title: What fits the hour
body: Stopping porn leaves a gap in the day. “Find a hobby” sounds sensible until it’s eleven at night and you have no idea what to begin. Choose something you can start at the hour you usually watch.
Ask what you need then. After a late shift, you might need food and rest. On an empty afternoon, you might want company or something interesting to do.
An activity can be enjoyable without improving you. A game with a friend, a meal, a walk, or a film can belong in your evening.

pages.title: Make it easier to begin
body: Katherine Milkman and her colleagues tested whether audiobooks could make gym visits more appealing. Participants in one group could listen to the supplied books only at the gym.
That group initially attended more often, but the advantage weakened over time, especially after a holiday break.
The experiment concerned exercise attendance, not recovery. Its useful idea is modest: making an activity enjoyable can make it easier to begin.
You can use that idea without making every pleasure a reward. Play music you like while cooking.
Pick a game you’d enjoy even if it did nothing for recovery. Food, sleep, and contact with people remain needs; don’t withhold them to prove commitment.
Prepare the first step. Put the ingredients out, leave the book on the chair, or agree on a time to play. The familiar habit already has an easy beginning. Your replacement needs one too.

pages.title: Try it and see
body: Try it for fifteen or twenty minutes today. Afterwards, ask what happened. Did you start? Did you enjoy it? Did it suit that particular hour?
Those are different questions. Cooking might work on Sunday and feel impossible after a late shift. Keep it for Sunday and choose something simpler for work nights.
If an activity helps once, try it again. If it doesn’t, change it. The gym study’s fading effect is a reminder to look beyond the first burst of interest.
You’re choosing things you’d like to keep doing after the novelty wears off.

pages.text: No man is free who is not master of himself.

pages.title: Have another activity ready
body: Choose an activity for the hour when you usually want porn. Match it to what you need: rest, interest, company, movement, or a break.

Prepare the materials and try it for fifteen to twenty minutes. Write whether it was easy to start and whether it helped you stop the usual browsing. Save it under Alternatives, with one adjustment if needed.
pages.done: You’ve tried the activity and recorded what happened. An unhelpful result is worth recording too.

pages.title: Lesson complete.
pages.body: One thing left today — the task.

pages.text: Man is by nature a social animal.

pages.title: Time alone
body: Being alone can be pleasant. Spending every evening avoiding messages and watching porn may feel different. Look at how your time alone is going before deciding that you need more of it or less.

items.t: Talking to a stranger would be less pleasant
Talking was more positive, on average

body: In experiments by Nicholas Epley and Juliana Schroeder, train and bus commuters were asked to speak with a stranger, keep to themselves, or travel as usual.
Those assigned to speak reported a more positive experience on average than those assigned to stay alone. People making predictions had expected the opposite.
The finding doesn’t promise that every conversation will go well. It suggests that an awkward prediction can sometimes be less accurate than a respectful attempt.

pages.title: A small attempt
body: A small attempt is enough today. Ask someone about their week. Suggest a short call. Invite a friend to do something at a particular time.
“Want to play on Thursday evening?” is easier to answer than “We should hang out sometime.”
You don’t have to explain your porn use. An ordinary conversation can give an isolated evening some company.

If you want support with recovery, ask separately and say what would help: listening for ten minutes, joining you for a walk, or helping you find a clinician. Let the person decide what they can offer.

pages.title: While you wait
body: Have something else to do if they’re busy. Sending an invitation and staring at the phone all evening can make the attempt feel much more loaded than it needs to be.
Leave room for a reply and carry on with your plans. Silence alone doesn’t tell you what the other person thinks of you.
If you have no safe person to contact, check a class, club, community group, or suitable support service. Find out how to attend and what it costs.
A regular meeting gives you another chance to see the same people. Friendship usually needs time and effort from both sides. Today, your part is to make one reasonable beginning.

pages.text: What brings no benefit to the hive brings none to the bee.

pages.title: Make time for contact
body: Call someone, send a specific invitation, or spend time in a conversation or shared activity. Choose contact that’s safe and appropriate.
If no personal contact is available, check how to join a regular group or access a suitable service.
Save one option under Support. After an unanswered invitation, leave room for a reply and continue another activity.
pages.done: You’ve taken a contact step or checked a group or service you can access. You don’t need a reply to finish.

pages.title: Lesson complete.
pages.body: One thing left today — the task.

pages.text: It is not that we have a short time to live, but that we waste much of it.

pages.title: What made a difference
body: This week gave you several things to try. The useful question now is which of them made a difference in your actual evenings. You don’t need to make the answer encouraging.
Suppose the phone stayed across the room on two nights. On the third, you brought it back because you couldn’t hear the alarm. “I have no discipline” misses a detail you can fix.
A louder alarm or a different shelf might help. But “moving the phone solved everything” also says more than three nights can show.
Look at what happened after each change. Did you leave the phone where you put it? Did you stop browsing when you planned?
Could you start the activity you had ready? If something helped, name the part that helped. If it didn’t, name what got in the way.

pages.title: Quiet nights and hard ones
body: There’s a difference between preparing something and using it during an urge. A quiet night can show that the phone’s new charging place is convenient.
It can’t yet tell you how you’ll respond on a harder night. Write what you know and leave the rest open. That will make the next decision easier.
Review the sleep plan from Day 4 too. Was the stopping time realistic? Did work run late? Did the quieter activity help you stay out of the feed?
Keep what fitted your life and change one thing that didn’t. Several changes at once can make it hard to tell what mattered.

pages.title: Next week
body: If nothing helped clearly, choose one small change to try next week. If the problem still seriously affects your life, use the support contact you saved. Help doesn’t have to wait until Day 84.
Then do something you enjoy. Have a meal, watch a film, play a game, or spend time with someone. A slip this week doesn’t take that away.
The course should help you spend more time living your life, including the parts that don’t need a lesson attached to them.

options.t: Keeping my phone away at night
Removing saved material or changing where I browse
Going outside or moving to another room
Preparing for sleep
Having another activity ready
Spending time with someone
Another change

pages.lead: Keep what helped, or make one awkward part easier to begin.
body: If nothing has helped and the problem is seriously affecting life, seek more support.

pages.text: The impediment to action advances action. What stands in the way becomes the way.

pages.title: Review the first week
body: Read your plan for five minutes. Name one change you used and what happened. Check the sleep plan from Day 4 and the activity from Day 5. Keep what helped or change one awkward detail.
If nothing helped clearly, record the obstacle and choose one change for next week. Then do something you enjoy within your means.
pages.done: You’ve recorded the review and taken time for enjoyment. A slip during the week doesn’t cancel that time.

pages.body: Your answers are saved to the log. One thing left today — the task.

pages.text: Not everything that can be counted counts, and not everything that counts can be counted.

pages.title: What a streak leaves out
body: A streak tells you how many days in a row you’ve kept a rule. That can be encouraging. But it leaves out a lot of what happens in those days.

items.t: Argues with the urge in bed until exhausted
Puts the phone away earlier and gets back to the evening

body: Imagine two people who haven’t watched porn for two weeks. One spends every night in bed arguing with the urge until they’re exhausted.
The other puts the phone away earlier and gets back to a game, a conversation, or sleep. The counters match. Their evenings don’t.

pages.title: One more measure
body: Researchers led by Benjamin Harkin reviewed 138 experiments on monitoring progress towards different goals. Monitoring helped goal achievement on average, though the studies covered many kinds of goals and weren’t a test of this course.
The point for you is to record something that helps you make a decision, rather than record more for its own sake.
Choose one measure beyond the streak. You might note how much time watching took, whether the phone stayed out of bed, or whether you used the steps you planned when an urge appeared.
Keep it brief. If the number is unknown, write “unknown.” A guess dressed up as a measurement won’t help later.

pages.title: What the record is for
body: After a slip, the earlier nights still happened. The charger you moved is still there.
The activity you enjoyed is still available. A counter restarting doesn’t erase those things. Look at what you can use again today.
Results can also be mixed. Perhaps you’re watching less but staying up late on another feed. Perhaps urges remain strong, but you’re ending searches sooner.
Those differences matter because they point to different next steps. Sleep needs attention in the first example; remembering to act earlier may matter in the second.
Check your notes when you need to decide what to keep or change. If logging starts taking over the day or making you repeatedly check yourself, simplify it.
A few useful facts are enough. The record should help you understand an evening, then let you get on with it.

pages.text: Measure what is measurable, and make measurable what is not so.

pages.title: Measure more than a streak
body: Choose one measure besides a streak: time spent watching, nights with the phone out of bed, or whether you used your response to an urge.
Record what you know about the last seven days, with unknown for gaps. Then repeat one useful action today, or try a small version if you’re still finding what helps.
pages.done: The measure and starting information are saved, and you’ve tried one action.

pages.body: One thing left today — the task.

pages.text: Our greatest glory is not in never falling, but in rising every time we fall.

pages.title: The next hour
body: You’ve watched porn after deciding not to. The next thought may be, “The streak is gone, so I might as well carry on.” That thought can turn a short episode into a lost night.
The next hour still has something in it. You might sleep, eat, keep an appointment, or finish a task.
Closing the screen now keeps more of those things possible. You can look at why you watched later, when you’re less tired and the content is closed.

pages.title: The first half-hour
body: Think about what usually happens in the first half-hour after a slip. Do you keep searching? Start insulting yourself? Cancel plans?
Stay awake reading advice? One of those actions may be adding more trouble than the first decision did. Choose where you’ll stop that part next time.

steps: Leave the phone on the shelf

body: For a late-night episode, the steps could be simple: close the content, leave the phone on the shelf, wash, and get ready for bed.
For an afternoon, you might put the laptop away and make lunch. Write steps that fit the hour. A long walk isn’t helpful as your only answer if you can’t leave home at midnight.
Ending an episode doesn’t mean pretending it had no consequences. If you missed work or broke an agreement, that may need attention.
Deal with the immediate problem first, then choose a specific repair or ask for help. Repeating “I’m terrible” doesn’t tell you how to do either.

pages.title: Keep it short
body: Use a recent example if you have one. If you haven’t slipped, prepare the steps for a possible future episode. There is no reason to create a mistake so you can practise recovering from it.
Keep the note short enough to read when you’re upset. Put the first action at the top.
The purpose is to help you stop sooner and resume the day, without needing to feel forgiven, motivated, or certain before you begin.

pages.text: A gem cannot be polished without friction, nor a man perfected without trials.

pages.title: Stop sooner after a slip
body: Add After a slip to your plan. Using a recent example if available, note what you did in the first thirty minutes.
Then write the steps you want to use: close the content, put the device in a named place, and begin the next necessary activity.
Choose the activity for the likely hour, such as food, work, or bed. If you haven’t slipped, prepare the steps for a possible episode without creating one.
pages.done: The plan names the first action, device location, and what you’ll do next.

pages.title: Lesson complete.
pages.body: One thing left today — the task.

pages.text: The perfect is the enemy of the good.

pages.title: Look at what’s left
body: One missed session becomes a reason to stop training. A late start becomes a reason to abandon work.
A slip becomes permission to keep watching. The original mistake gets bigger because the next decision treats the day as already lost.
Listen for the sentence that does this: “I’ll start Monday,” “There’s no point now,” or “I’ve ruined it.” Then look at what’s actually left.

At eleven at night, you can still prepare for bed. At eleven in the morning, you can still eat breakfast and begin a piece of work. The answer depends on the hour, not on making the day look perfect again.

items.t: Tomorrow starts with even less sleep
The next hour can be used differently

body: Suppose you watched for twenty minutes after a difficult shift. If you keep searching for another hour, tomorrow starts with even less sleep.
If you close it now, those twenty minutes remain a mistake, but the next hour can be used differently. That difference is worth protecting.

pages.title: Check the details
body: Today, try the steps you wrote yesterday while you aren’t dealing with an urge. Close a harmless tab, put the device where you planned, and move to the room or activity you chose.
Check the details. Can you hear the alarm? Is the kitchen available? Does the next activity need something you haven’t prepared?
Fix one awkward step. A plan that says “go outside” needs an indoor option if going out at night is unsafe.
A plan that says “call a friend” needs something to do if the friend is busy. The easier beginning is often more useful than stronger promises.

pages.title: Two different tests
body: This practice shows whether you can follow the instructions in your room.
When you use them during an urge, you’ll learn something else: whether they help you stop and move on. Keep those two observations separate.
If today is going well, let it keep going well. You can practise the steps without ruining anything first. Returning after a mistake is a skill worth preparing, not a mistake you need to manufacture.

pages.prompt: You watched late at night after deciding not to. What helps with the rest of the night?

options.t: Close the content and follow the steps for bed
Keep watching because the streak has ended
Stay awake reviewing every detail before putting the phone away

pages.label: Best answer

best.t: Close the content and follow the steps for bed

body: Stop watching first and review what happened later.

pages.text: Better a diamond with a flaw than a pebble without.

pages.title: Use the hours that remain
body: Try the after-slip steps once without an urge. Close a harmless tab, put the device where you planned, and move to the named room or activity.
Check whether it fits the hour when you usually watch. Fix one obstacle, such as an unavailable room or an unsafe late-night walk. Use an accessible option if moving isn’t possible.
pages.done: You’ve tried the steps and corrected an obstacle if needed. No sexual content or induced urge is needed.

pages.title: Lesson complete.
pages.body: Your answers are saved to the log. One thing left today — the task.

title: Try one change for a week

pages.text: The path up and the path down are one and the same.

pages.title: The whole week
body: An unusually easy evening can make you feel the problem is solved. A difficult one can make you feel nothing has changed. Neither evening tells the whole story.
Look at the last week. How much time did you spend watching? What happened when you noticed an urge? How did you respond after a slip or a missed task?
Compare that with the starting notes you wrote on Day 1. Keep the comparison as specific as the notes allow.

pages.title: Different problems

head: What happens
What it needs
rows: You notice sooner, but can’t put the phone down
You notice only half an hour into searching

body: For example, you might be noticing the urge sooner but still struggling to put the phone down. That’s different from not noticing until you’ve been searching for half an hour.
The first problem needs help with beginning the next action. The second needs a clearer warning sign, such as opening a particular account.
You might also be watching less while still losing sleep to unrelated videos. That is a mixed result, and it deserves to stay mixed in the record.
Praising the reduction while ignoring the lost sleep would leave you with the wrong next task.

pages.title: One change for seven days
body: If the starting notes are thin, say so. “I used to watch most nights, but I didn’t record the time” is enough. You can start a clearer note now. You don’t need to reconstruct every old evening from memory.
Choose one change to try for seven days. Maybe the evening activity needs an easier beginning, the browsing needs an earlier ending, or the charger needs a different place.
Change the detail that actually got in the way. Doing five new things at once makes the result harder to understand and gives you more to remember.
Put a Day 18 reminder in your notes or calendar. When it arrives, ask whether you tried the change and what happened.
If the situation never came up, you won’t have an answer yet. Wait until it does. Seven days gives you a time to check, not a reason to declare a result you haven’t seen.

pages.text: Nothing endures but change.

pages.title: Try one change for a week
body: Compare the past seven days with Day 1: time or disruption from porn, responses to urges or slips, and one daily routine. Include unchanged or unknown where accurate.
Choose one change for the next seven days. Prepare it today and save a Day 18 review reminder. Write what you want to learn from trying it.
pages.done: The comparison is written, the change is ready, and the review reminder is saved.

pages.title: Lesson complete.
pages.body: One thing left today — the task.

pages.text: Character is simply habit long continued.

pages.title: Something you do

items.t: “I keep watching longer than I intend.”

items.l: Claims to be everything you are
items.t: “I’m hopeless.”

body: “I keep watching longer than I intend” describes something you do. “I’m hopeless” claims to describe everything you are.
The first sentence gives you a problem to work on. The second makes the next attempt seem pointless.
You might prefer a more encouraging description, such as “I’m someone who takes care of my time.” If it helps, use it. But give it an action.
Put the phone away after brushing your teeth, or begin a short piece of work before opening a feed. Then you’ll know what keeping the commitment looks like.

pages.title: No fixed number of days
body: Phillippa Lally and her colleagues followed people repeating everyday behaviours over twelve weeks. The behaviours became more automatic at different speeds for different people.
Their findings don’t support a fixed number of days in which everybody forms a habit. A missed repetition is a reason to look at what happened, not proof that you’ve missed a universal deadline.
Consider someone who plans to read after dinner. On three nights they do. On a fourth, dinner happens elsewhere and the book is at home.
“I’m not a reader after all” explains nothing useful. Keeping the book in their bag might. Or they may choose a different cue on nights out.
Do the same with your commitment. If you forgot, choose a reminder you will see. If the action took too much effort, make the beginning smaller.
If the event you linked it to didn’t happen, decide how to handle that day. Those answers are easier to use than a verdict about your character.

pages.title: One behaviour this week
body: Choose one behaviour for the next week and set a Day 19 reminder. You can keep the change from yesterday instead of adding another. Repeating one action is enough work if that action matters.
The notes can stay simple: did it happen, and what got in the way? Over time, they may give you reasons to trust the commitment.
You won’t need to argue yourself into believing a larger claim about who you’ve become.

pages.text: How long are you going to wait before you demand the best for yourself?

pages.title: Repeat one useful action
body: Choose one behaviour to repeat for a week. You can keep the Day 11 change. Write the cue and action, such as putting the phone away after brushing your teeth.
Prepare what it needs and try it when the cue occurs. If it hasn’t occurred, name the first expected chance. Record missed attempts honestly and set a Day 19 review.
pages.done: The behaviour, first chance, setup, and review are clear.

pages.title: Lesson complete.
pages.body: One thing left today — the task.

pages.text: He who knows others is wise; he who knows himself is enlightened.

pages.title: Your reason
body: Why do you want to change your porn use? Your answer might be sleep, time, a relationship agreement, faith, or difficulty stopping when you want to. Start there. You don’t need to borrow somebody else’s reason.
Beatrice, whose smoking story is published by the CDC, described how a letter from her son helped her decide to quit. She also used medication and support from people around her.
She had a personal reason to quit, alongside practical help. It doesn’t show that caring about someone is enough by itself, or that smoking treatment should be copied into this course.

pages.title: Words you’d recognise

items.t: “I want to stop losing sleep.”
“I need to become a better person.”

body: Give your own reason a sentence you could recognise on a tired evening. “I want to stop losing sleep” is clearer than “I need to become a better person.”
“I want to keep the agreement we made” points to a commitment you can discuss and follow. The wording doesn’t have to sound inspiring.
Guilt alone doesn’t tell you how severe the problem is. Moral disapproval by itself does not establish compulsive sexual behaviour disorder.

A personal or religious choice can still matter to you without being a diagnosis. If you have persistent difficulty controlling sexual behaviour and daily life is seriously affected, seek qualified assessment.
Ask whether the reason has turned into an insult. “I regret breaking our agreement” names a decision.
“I’m disgusting” attacks the whole person and leaves the agreement untouched. Bring the sentence back to what you want to do, protect, or repair.

pages.title: Act on it
body: Then give the reason some time today. If sleep matters, end browsing when you planned. If a relationship matters, give the person your attention or discuss the agreement honestly.
If faith matters, make time for a practice you freely choose. The action should follow your reason, rather than serve as punishment.

You may still be unsure. Keep the rule about your behaviour clear while you think. You can choose to stop watching without inventing damage, illness, or a dramatic explanation for why the choice matters.

options.t: To protect time or sleep
To have more control over what I do
To keep a relationship agreement
To follow a personal or religious value
Another reason
I’m still working out the reason

pages.lead: Write the reason in your own words and take one action that follows it.
body: If you’re unsure, keep the viewing rule clear while you think.

pages.text: No man is free who is not master of himself.

pages.title: Choose your own reason
body: Write one sentence under Goal explaining why you want to change porn use. Name a real effect or a value you choose to follow, without an insult about yourself.
Take one related action today: protect sleep, keep an agreement, give someone attention, or make time for a chosen faith or community activity. Make an arrangement if the action needs one.

pages.text: Difficulties strengthen the mind, as labour does the body.

pages.title: When the newness wears off
body: The newness wears off. The charger is in its new place, the lessons are familiar, and the first burst of motivation has passed. That is when a small routine needs to be easy enough to keep.
Choose how you’ll return after a missed day. Open the next lesson when you have time, do one useful action, and continue.
You don’t owe the course several extra lessons because yesterday was busy. Turning a missed day into a debt can make coming back feel much harder.
Suppose you miss two days while travelling. When you get home, you could restart Day 1 and announce a stricter plan.
Or you could put the phone back on its charging shelf and resume where you stopped. The second choice uses something you already prepared. You can improve it later if travel exposed a problem.

pages.title: Slips and low motivation
body: Keep a different answer ready for a slip. Use the steps in “After a slip,” then return to the next thing the day needs. Reading more isn’t always the next useful action. Late at night, sleep may matter more.
Low motivation also deserves a specific answer. Which part has been helping enough to keep? Perhaps the phone stays out of bed even on days you don’t feel like doing a lesson.
Keep that. If an exercise repeatedly doesn’t fit, change it instead of forcing another attempt for the sake of finishing.
Continuing also includes noticing when more help is needed.
If the course is making you more distressed, or control and daily life are getting worse, talk to a qualified professional. Repetition isn’t a reason to ignore that information.

pages.title: Three answers

rows: Open the next lesson, do one useful action, and continue
Use the after-a-slip steps, then the next thing the day needs
Keep the part that has been helping

body: Write the three answers briefly: what you’ll do after a missed lesson, after a slip, and when you don’t feel motivated. Use things you can actually begin.
Then close the notes and use the day. Staying with a change usually involves many unremarkable returns, not a constant feeling of resolve.

pages.text: It’s not what happens to you, but how you react to it that matters.

pages.title: Return after a missed day
body: Add three short answers under Continuing: when you’ll resume after a missed day, how you’ll use the after-slip steps, and which helpful behaviour you’ll keep when motivation is low.
Include who or which service you’ll contact if the course isn’t helping or daily life is getting worse. Adjust the pace when needed rather than make missed lessons a debt.
pages.done: Each situation has a specific next action in the plan.

title: What to do when an urge starts

pages.text: No state is so bitter that a calm mind cannot find in it some consolation.

pages.title: Before the reach
body: An urge can feel like a decision you’ve already made. You notice the familiar thought, reach for the phone, and start searching. The few seconds before that reach are worth paying attention to.
Try describing what happens without finishing the story for it. “I want to open that account” tells you more than “I’m going to relapse.”
The first sentence leaves room to put the phone down. The second can make watching feel inevitable.

pages.title: You don’t have to wait

viz.cap: You can act before the urge fades. It may come with you for a while.

body: Urges don’t follow a timetable. Some ease quickly; others return or stay uncomfortable. You don’t have to wait for the feeling to disappear before changing what you do.
Close the content, move the device, and begin the next activity you chose. The urge may come with you for a while.
Suppose you’re in bed and remember a video. The memory itself hasn’t broken your rule. Searching for it would be the next action.
Put the phone on the shelf and get ready for sleep. If you need another step, sit somewhere else briefly or read a few pages. Choose something you can actually do at that hour.

pages.title: The earliest sign
body: Look for the earliest sign you usually recognise. It might be opening a feed, switching to private browsing, or thinking “just a quick look.”
You needn’t catch the very first thought. Catching the sequence sooner than usual is still useful.
Write one sentence for that moment: “When I open that account, I’ll close it and put the phone on the kitchen counter.”
Keep the beginning specific. “Be strong” leaves you with another decision to make while you’re already tempted.
If no urge happens today, prepare the steps and practise putting the device away. Don’t search for material to test them. You can find out whether the steps help when an urge appears on its own.

pages.text: You have power over your mind, not outside events. Realize this, and you will find strength.

pages.title: What to do when an urge starts
body: Write your earliest recognisable sign of an urge and a first action under Early signs and First response. Then put the phone out of reach for five minutes without seeking a trigger.
At the start and end, notice the wish to check it. You can rate it from zero to ten. Record whether it changed, stayed the same, or wasn’t there. No thought or sensation has to appear.
pages.done: The cue and response are saved, and the short observation is recorded. Zero throughout is a valid result.

pages.text: The beginning of wisdom is the definition of terms.

pages.title: Start with the facts
body: What was happening before you wanted porn? Sometimes the answer is sexual desire.
Sometimes you’re tired, annoyed, avoiding work, or filling an empty evening. There may be several things going on, or no clear explanation.
Start with the facts. You came home late. You hadn’t eaten. A task was waiting. You opened the phone while sitting on the bed.
Those details give you more to work with than a theory about what every urge must mean.

pages.title: An action that fits

head: What you notice
What fits
rows: A first sentence, or a request for help
An invitation, and something to do while you wait

body: The next action should fit what you can identify. Hunger calls for food. A difficult email may need a first sentence or a request for help.
Wanting company may call for an invitation, with something else to do while you wait. None of those steps guarantees the urge will disappear. They deal with a problem that was there before it.
Imagine someone coming home after an argument. Watching might postpone the conversation for an hour, but the disagreement will still need attention.
Tonight they could stop browsing, eat, and decide when to speak again. Trying to solve the whole relationship while upset is a much larger task.

You also don’t need a hidden emotional explanation for every sexual feeling. If desire is the main thing you notice, keep the porn rule clear and decide separately how you want to handle masturbation or intimacy.
Another person’s interest and consent matter; sex isn’t a task somebody else owes you.

pages.title: Name one need
body: Today, name one likely need and one action that fits it. If you’re unsure, write “unsure” and use the simple steps you’ve already prepared. Analysis can wait until you’ve closed the content.
Later, check what happened. Perhaps lunch helped with hunger but didn’t change the urge. That’s useful information. You met one need and still had to choose what to do with the feeling.

pages.prompt: What was happening before a recent urge?
pages.instr: Choose all that fit. Choose H alone if it fits.

options.t: Sexual desire
Boredom or wanting something interesting
Tiredness or wanting rest
Loneliness or wanting company
Avoiding a task
Anger or another difficult feeling
Something else
No recent example or no clear explanation

body: Choose an action for one need you can identify. If you don’t know, save the question for the next urge that happens naturally.

pages.text: Know thyself.
pages.by: Inscription at the Temple of Apollo at Delphi

pages.title: Check what you need
body: For a recent urge, note the time and place, what you were doing beforehand, how you felt physically, and your mood or any task you were avoiding. Unknown or nothing obvious is fine.
Choose one action for a need you can identify and try it if that need is present. If no example comes to mind, save the questions for the next urge that happens naturally.
pages.done: The facts and next action are saved, or the questions are ready for later.

pages.body: Your answers are saved to the log. One thing left today — the task.

pages.text: Walking is man’s best medicine.

pages.title: Move before you’ve decided
body: You don’t always have to settle the argument in your head before standing up. Closing the laptop and moving to the kitchen can happen while part of you still wants to keep watching.
Movement helps here because it interrupts what you’re doing. The new room gives you a chance to start something else.
It isn’t a guaranteed way to remove an urge, and it doesn’t need to be strenuous. Standing, wheeling to another space, or putting the device out of reach may be enough to change the next action.

pages.title: Rehearse where it happens
body: Think about where urges usually happen. If it’s the sofa after work, rehearse from the sofa. Put the phone down, get up, and go where you planned.
Find the awkward detail now. Are your shoes elsewhere? Is the kitchen occupied? Does the next activity require a device you’ve just put away?
Fix the beginning rather than making the promise bigger. Keep a book beside the chair. Prepare a drink. Choose an indoor activity when going out isn’t possible.
If leaving the room would be unsafe or inaccessible, close the content and change the position of the device instead.

pages.title: When the urge arrives
body: When an urge arrives, use the first step before negotiating how long you might watch.
You can still feel tempted while making tea or opening your coursework. Give the next activity a few minutes before deciding whether to change it.
Today, try the steps once without an urge. That checks whether the instructions fit your home and circumstances.
It doesn’t establish that they’ll work every time you’re tempted. After actual use, record whether you stopped watching and what helped or got in the way.
If moving rooms repeatedly leaves you opening the same material elsewhere, change what happens after the move. The room was only the beginning. You still need something to do there.

pages.text: Action is the antidote to despair.

pages.title: Close the screen and move
body: Start where you usually browse. Close a harmless tab, put the device away, and move to the place or activity in your First response. Fix anything that makes beginning awkward.
At the next naturally occurring urge, try the steps and record what happened. If none occurs today, leave them ready.
pages.done: You’ve practised the movement and saved any adjustment. The result during an urge can be recorded later.

pages.text: The soul becomes dyed with the colour of its thoughts.

pages.title: The first minute
body: Changing what you do works best when you’ve prepared the first minute. “Find something else” is hard to follow when the phone is already in your hand.
Look back at the change you chose on Day 11. Did you try it? Did the situation happen? What made it easier or harder?
If the week never included the evening you planned for, keep the reminder for the next time. There isn’t a result to report yet.

pages.title: When the beginning isn’t ready

items.t: Ingredients ready. You began cooking.
Hungry, fridge empty. You reached for the phone.

body: Suppose you planned to cook after work instead of browsing in bed. On Tuesday you had ingredients and began. On Thursday you were hungry, the fridge was empty, and you reached for the phone.
The useful change may be keeping an easy meal available. Cooking wasn’t necessarily the wrong choice; its beginning wasn’t ready.
Other addictions offer practical examples of preparation. GamCare’s gambling guidance includes tools such as self-exclusion and planning for difficult situations.
These approaches address access and decisions in advance. They don’t show that gambling and porn use have the same causes or need the same treatment.

pages.title: Your next difficult hour
body: For your next difficult hour, choose an activity that fits the need you noticed. Prepare what it takes to begin. If it’s company, make an invitation and have another activity ready while you wait.
If it’s rest, avoid replacing browsing with a demanding workout. If it’s a delayed task, choose the first manageable part.
You can keep the change from Day 11 when it’s helping. You don’t need a new technique because the calendar has reached a new lesson.
If it failed, change one detail and check it after you’ve had a chance to use it.

An alternative may feel less immediately appealing than porn. It can still be worth doing. Judge whether it helped you stop and use the time as you intended, rather than whether it produced the same feeling.

pages.prompt: What happened with the change you chose on Day 11?

options.t: I tried it and it helped at least once
I tried it but it didn’t clearly help
I couldn’t get started
The situation I planned for didn’t happen
I don’t have enough information to judge

pages.lead: Keep a helpful detail or change one part that got in the way.
body: If the situation hasn’t happened, check after it does. If information is missing, start a brief note now.

pages.text: The happiness of your life depends upon the quality of your thoughts.

pages.title: Prepare another activity
body: Review the Day 11 change: did you try it, what happened, and will you keep or change it? If the situation didn’t happen, move the check to after it does.
Prepare an activity you can begin quickly, one that can hold your attention longer, and a contact or shared-place option.
Use things you like or need. Get the materials or details ready and try the quickest option once.

title: Check hunger, anger, loneliness, and tiredness

pages.text: The body should be treated more rigorously, that it may not be disobedient to the mind.

pages.title: A short checklist
body: HALT is a reminder to check whether you’re hungry, angry, lonely, or tired. It’s a short checklist, not an explanation for every urge.

rows: Step away before deciding what to say
A safe contact or a shared activity
Prepare for the next sleep period

body: The check should lead somewhere simple. If you haven’t eaten, get food. If you’re tired, prepare for the next sleep period.
If you’re angry, step away from the argument before deciding what to say. If you’re lonely, consider a safe contact or a shared activity. Several answers can fit at once.
There will also be times when none fits. You may be rested, fed, and still want porn. Use the steps you’ve prepared instead of forcing the feeling into one of four boxes.
Sexual desire doesn’t need to be renamed hunger or loneliness before you can choose what to do.

pages.title: Review your behaviour
body: Review the behaviour you chose on Day 12. Did you repeat it when the cue happened? If you forgot, place a reminder where you’ll see it.
If it was too much for the evening, shorten the beginning. If the cue didn’t occur, wait for a real chance before judging the habit.
Consider a late shift. You might have planned to go running after work, then arrive home hungry and exhausted.
Eating and going to bed could be the better decision that night. Keeping the larger goal doesn’t require treating every tired evening as a test of character.

pages.title: Separate questions
body: For today’s practice, choose the next action from the facts in front of you. Make it small enough to begin now.
Close the triggering material first; checking how you feel while continuing to browse leaves the main action unchanged.
Afterwards, note whether the basic need was met and whether you kept the porn boundary. Those are separate questions.
A meal can help with hunger even if the urge remains. You can continue choosing your actions while it does.

pages.instr: Choose all that fit. Choose E or F alone if it fits.

options.t: Hunger
Anger

pages.text: Before you heal someone, ask him if he’s willing to give up the things that made him sick.

pages.title: Check hunger, anger, loneliness, and tiredness
body: Review the Day 12 behaviour: attempts, obstacles, and what to keep or change. If you haven’t had a chance to try it, keep the review for afterwards.
Check hunger, anger, loneliness, and tiredness now. Mark present, absent, or unsure. Take a fitting action if one needs attention. If none fits, record that instead of forcing an explanation.

title: Notice an urge without acting on it

pages.text: You can’t stop the waves, but you can learn to surf.

pages.title: What urge surfing is
body: Urge surfing means noticing an urge without immediately acting on it. The name can sound more complicated than the exercise. You’re making room for a feeling while keeping your hands off the search button.

items.t: No clear drop in the mindfulness group
Fewer in the mindfulness group

body: In a study of 123 student smokers, Sarah Bowen and Alan Marlatt tested brief mindfulness instructions. Reported urges didn’t clearly fall more in the mindfulness group, but that group reported fewer cigarettes over the following week.
It was a short smoking study, not proof about this course. It does illustrate why feeling less craving and smoking less are different outcomes.

pages.title: How to try it
body: If you’d like to try the exercise, close the content first. Sit or stand somewhere comfortable and notice what’s present: a thought, restlessness, tightness, or the wish to reach for the phone.
You don’t have to find a bodily sensation. Breathe normally and let the feeling be there for a minute or two without searching.
Then begin the next thing you’ve chosen. Put the phone away, make food, return to work, or prepare for bed. The exercise needs that ending.
Watching the feeling indefinitely can turn a short pause into another long evening spent thinking about porn.
If paying attention to sensations makes you more distressed or absorbed in the urge, stop.
Use a different response, such as changing rooms or asking for support. This is an option, not a requirement to sit through escalating discomfort.

pages.title: What to record
body: You can practise the steps when you aren’t tempted. That teaches you how to do them, but won’t tell you yet whether they help during an urge. Don’t deliberately expose yourself to content to find out.
When you do use the exercise, record the next action. Did you close the content and move on?
The urge may have eased, stayed, or returned. Keep that detail honest without making disappearance the condition for success.

pages.prompt: After three minutes of noticing an urge, it still feels strong. What can you do?

options.t: Decide the exercise has definitely failed
Begin the next action even while the urge remains
Keep observing until the urge disappears

pages.label: Best answer

best.t: Begin the next action even while the urge remains

body: The feeling and what you do next are different things. Stop observing if it isn’t helping.

pages.text: The nearer a man comes to a calm mind, the closer he is to strength.

pages.title: Notice an urge without acting on it
body: Close triggering content. For two to five minutes, notice a mild urge that has appeared naturally, or practise without one.
Notice thoughts or sensations if present, breathe normally, and return attention when it wanders.
Finish by beginning the next action you chose. Record the feeling and what you did separately.
Use paper or memory if the phone is away. Stop and choose another response if the exercise is uncomfortable or unhelpful.
pages.done: You’ve tried the steps and recorded the result, or stopped and chosen another response. An urge isn’t required.

title: Make a separate choice about masturbation

pages.text: Nothing in excess.

pages.title: Two separate choices
body: Porn and masturbation are separate behaviours. A course about changing porn use should make that distinction clear.
For some people, masturbation without porn fits the change they want. For others, it repeatedly leads to searching or becomes difficult to stop.
Some prefer abstinence for personal reasons. Choose a rule you can describe and later review, rather than assume one answer suits everyone.
Look at what actually happens. Can you keep the device away? Do you start searching afterwards?
Are you choosing freely, or spending more time than you intended and missing things that matter? These questions give you something to assess without declaring ordinary desire a disease.

pages.title: A rule you can review
body: You might choose, for now, not to use porn and not to take the phone into a private place where you usually search.
You might also decide to pause masturbation while you work out a recurring problem. State the rule plainly and set a time to reconsider it on Day 35.
Avoid turning the review into a hunt for danger in every thought. Attraction, a dream, or an unwanted memory isn’t an action crossing your boundary.
If an explicit image appears accidentally, close or move past it. The decision after exposure matters more than finding a label for the exposure itself.

pages.title: Partners and your own rule
body: If you have a partner, any change involving them needs discussion and consent. Sex isn’t an emergency replacement for porn, and a partner isn’t responsible for making your urges disappear.
A rule about your own viewing can be followed even when someone else isn’t available or interested.
Today, write the boundary in one or two sentences. Prepare the device or room if that makes following it easier. On Day 35, look at what happened and decide whether to keep or change the rule.
If control remains difficult and life is seriously affected, ask for qualified help. You don’t need to settle every sexual decision alone before making that request.

pages.text: The first and best victory is to conquer self.

pages.title: Make a separate choice about masturbation
body: Write your choice about masturbation separately from the porn boundary. Keep a choice that fits your values and experience.
If masturbation repeatedly leads to searching, consider keeping devices away or a temporary pause.
If unsure, keep porn out of it and observe only if masturbation happens. Prepare any device change and set a Day 35 review. Add qualified support if sexual behaviour remains difficult to control.
pages.done: The choice, setup, and review date are saved. No sexual activity is required.

pages.body: One thing left today — the task.

pages.text: Nature does nothing in vain.

pages.title: More than a pleasure tank
body: Dopamine helps with learning and motivation. It isn’t simply a tank of pleasure that porn drains and abstinence refills.
Neuroscientist Joshua Berke’s review describes several roles for dopamine, including how it relates to reward and the effort to pursue it.
The everyday lesson is easier to follow than a brain story. When a familiar activity repeatedly gives you something you want, reminders of it can prompt you to begin.
The phone, the account, and the hour may become part of that habit.

pages.title: Wanting isn’t enjoying
body: Wanting also isn’t the same as enjoying. You might keep searching while feeling bored or disappointed.
Ask what you’re doing and what it’s giving you now, rather than assuming the intensity of the urge proves the activity will be satisfying.

items.t: You want a break.
Switching accounts, still waiting for something good.

body: Think about opening a feed after a long day. At first you want a break. Half an hour later, you’re switching between accounts and still waiting for something good.
Closing it may feel difficult even though the last few minutes haven’t been pleasant. That discrepancy is useful to notice.

pages.title: Change one reminder
body: Today, choose one reminder you can change before the difficult hour: the phone beside the bed, a saved account, or the moment you open a feed after work.
Keep the change specific. You can’t make every cue disappear, but you can stop leaving the easiest one ready.
Then prepare another use for the time. A walk, meal, conversation, or hobby has its own value. It doesn’t need to provide an equivalent burst of stimulation to deserve a place in your day.
Save a brief note for Day 28: what you changed, whether you used the change, and what happened.
You won’t need to claim that your brain has reset. What matters here is whether the evening became easier to spend as you intended.

pages.prompt: Which detail helps you change the habit?

options.t: Guessing how damaged my dopamine system is
The account, time, or place where browsing begins
Ranking all enjoyable activities as good or bad dopamine

pages.label: Best answer

best.t: The account, time, or place where browsing begins

body: It names something you can change. The course doesn’t measure dopamine or diagnose brain damage.

pages.text: We are what we repeatedly do.

pages.title: Understand what starts the habit
body: Choose one account, feed, time, or device location that starts the habit. Change what you can without reopening porn. If access is already reduced, check whether the setup held and fix one inconvenience.
Save the cue and first action under Early signs. Set a Day 28 check.
pages.done: You’ve addressed a remaining cue or confirmed what works, and saved the review.

pages.body: Your answers are saved to the log. One thing left today — the task.

pages.text: The mind is not a vessel to be filled, but a fire to be kindled.

pages.title: Decide in advance
body: Planning ahead helps because it removes a decision you would otherwise have to make while tired or tempted. You can choose where the phone goes before you’re in bed arguing about another five minutes.

rows: I open that account after dinner
I’ll close it and put the phone on the shelf

body: One form is an if then plan: “If I open that account after dinner, I’ll close it and put the phone on the shelf.” The cue is something you can recognise. The response begins with an action you can perform.

pages.title: Plans that fit
body: Gollwitzer and Brandstätter studied plans that specify when and where to act. In a holiday report-writing task, those who made plans were more likely to finish among participants who returned the follow-up.
Some original participants didn’t return it. The finding supports taking planning seriously; it doesn’t guarantee that a sentence will solve a difficult habit.
The plan still needs to fit the room. “I’ll call a friend” leaves you waiting if they’re busy.
“I’ll put the phone away, make tea, and send an invitation tomorrow” includes something you control now. A useful first step doesn’t depend on getting an immediate reply.

pages.title: Write and test one
body: Write one plan for the point where you usually start. Avoid “Whenever I feel bad, I’ll do something healthy.”
Neither half tells you exactly what to notice or begin. Opening an account, getting into bed, or finishing dinner is easier to recognise.
Try the steps once without an urge. Put the device away and begin the next activity. If you need materials, get them ready. If the action is too long, shorten the beginning.
When the cue next happens, follow the plan and see what gets in the way. Forgetting means you may need a visible reminder.
Following it but returning to porn means the next activity or support may need attention. Those are different problems, and the notes can help you tell them apart.

pages.text: Forethought we may have, undoubtedly, but not foresight.

pages.title: Decide before the difficult hour
body: Make one decision ahead of the difficult hour. Write the cue and first action: where the phone goes or what you’ll begin after a named event.
Prepare the charger, materials, or short instructions. Try the beginning with harmless content. If an app or device is unavailable, prepare a paper or accessible alternative.
pages.done: The cue is clear, the materials are ready, and you’ve tried the beginning or prepared the needed alternative.

title: Make room for food and sleep

pages.text: If you would make a man happy, add not to his riches but take away from his desires.

pages.title: Basic care
body: Hunger and tiredness can make an evening harder to manage. They also deserve attention in their own right. You don’t need to prove that every urge came from them before eating or going to bed.
Look at the hours you usually struggle. Have you missed a meal? Are you staying awake after you intended to sleep?
Would the action you planned take more energy than you have? A demanding workout at midnight may make less sense than food, washing, and bed.

pages.title: Protect a realistic sleep
body: The sleep study on Day 4 found that repeated short sleep reduced attention even when people’s ratings of sleepiness didn’t fully reflect the decline.

Feeling that you can manage another hour awake isn’t a reliable reason to keep postponing sleep. That finding doesn’t explain every lapse in judgement, but it gives you a reason to protect a realistic sleep period.
Prepare for the actual constraints. If you work late, keep an easy meal available. If you’re caring for someone, choose the rest you can get rather than a schedule you can’t follow.
If a phone must remain nearby for calls or accessibility, keep those functions and put unrelated browsing out of the way.

pages.title: Add what’s missing
body: Use the Day 22 change if it’s already helping. Today doesn’t need another device rule. Add the missing basic care: food before the difficult hour, a stopping time for browsing, or a simpler evening activity.
Try the change once and save a note for Day 28. Record what you did, not what you assume it did to the brain.
“I ate before sitting down and put the phone away at eleven” is enough to compare with another evening.
Food and sleep aren’t punishments to earn through abstinence. After a slip, you still need them.
Taking care of the next hour gives tomorrow a better starting point, whether today’s record is encouraging or disappointing.

pages.text: Take care of the body with steadfast fidelity.

pages.title: Make room for food and sleep
body: Look at two or three difficult moments if you have examples. Was hunger or tiredness present? If so, try one practical change: an easy meal, eating earlier, or ending browsing in time for rest.
If neither fits or you don’t know, keep normal care and note what to check next time. Save a Day 28 reminder.
pages.done: You’ve tried a fitting change or saved an observation for later, with a review date.

pages.body: One thing left today — the task.

pages.text: Anger, if not restrained, is frequently more hurtful to us than the injury that provokes it.

pages.title: Name the problem
body: Anger and loneliness can lead you towards an activity that asks little of you and changes the feeling quickly.
If porn has served that purpose, simply removing it may leave the difficult part of the evening untouched.
Name the problem as closely as you can. “I’m angry about what happened at work” differs from “Nobody cares about me.”
The first suggests a situation you might address. The second may be how the evening feels, but it makes a much larger claim than the facts support.

pages.title: Angry or lonely
body: When angry, begin by stopping the actions likely to make things worse. Close the content. Step away from the argument or message draft.
Eat or rest if needed. Later, decide whether to ask a question, set a limit, or repair something you said.
When lonely, choose a kind of contact that fits. You may need more people around, a closer conversation, or support for losing someone particular.
A busy feed doesn’t necessarily provide any of those. An invitation or a regular group can be a beginning, though another person’s reply can’t be scheduled by you.
Suppose a friend cancels. You could take the cancellation as proof you’re unwanted and spend the night searching.
You could also make a new invitation for another day and use tonight for an activity you enjoy. The disappointment can remain without deciding the rest of the evening.

pages.title: Now and later
body: Today, choose one immediate action and, if needed, one later action on the actual problem. Put a time beside the later step so it doesn’t become another vague intention.
If the feeling is persistent, overwhelming, or affecting daily life, consider appropriate support.
A course exercise doesn’t need to become your only answer. You can work on porn use while also getting help for a difficulty that extends beyond it.

pages.text: We suffer more often in imagination than in reality.

pages.title: Respond to anger and loneliness
body: For a known example of anger or loneliness, write what happened and one immediate response.
For anger, that might be stepping away safely or delaying a message. For loneliness, try appropriate contact or check a regular shared activity.
Add a later step on the actual problem if needed. If neither feeling fits, leave the exercise aside or work with another feeling you’ve noticed.
pages.done: One fitting response is prepared or tried, or you’ve recorded that the topic doesn’t apply.

pages.title: Lesson complete.
pages.body: One thing left today — the task.

pages.text: The eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing.

pages.title: The next one
body: “Maybe the next one will be better” can keep a search going after you meant to stop. The next clip or account promises something different, so ending feels like giving up just before finding it.

items.t: Less pleasant than wins
Increase the wish to keep playing

body: A gambling experiment by Luke Clark and colleagues helps illustrate one part of this. Near misses could increase the wish to keep playing even though they were less pleasant than wins, especially when people had chosen the play themselves.
It was a specific gambling task, not a study of porn. Wanting another attempt and enjoying the result were different things.

pages.title: Enjoying or searching?
body: Look for that difference in your own browsing. Are you enjoying what you’re watching, or mostly trying to find something more satisfying?
You don’t have to keep searching until the activity becomes unpleasant enough to justify stopping. The time you intended to stop is already a reason.
Choose an earlier stopping point: opening the search bar, switching accounts again, or noticing that you’re bargaining for one more clip.
Use the sign that you actually recognise. A rule about the tenth video is less useful if you never count them.

pages.title: Where the search ends
body: Prepare the next action before you need it. Close the content, leave the device where you planned, and start the activity that fits the hour.
If you require the device for work, close the unnecessary tabs and open the specific task instead.
Today, practise stopping an unrelated, harmless feed when you intended to stop.
You are checking a practical detail: can you notice the time and begin something else? This doesn’t require seeking sexual content or reproducing the strongest urge.
Later, note what delayed you. Perhaps there was no clear ending, or the next activity wasn’t ready. Change that detail.
Calling the problem “novelty” may explain part of it, but the useful work is deciding where the search ends and what follows.

pages.prompt: What does the gambling near-miss experiment illustrate?

options.t: Wanting to continue can differ from enjoying what I’m doing
Porn and gambling always have the same effects and treatment
I need to keep searching until I find something satisfying

pages.label: Best answer

best.t: Wanting to continue can differ from enjoying what I’m doing

body: The study tested a gambling task. Look at your own experience to decide whether repeated searching is a problem for you.

pages.text: To be everywhere is to be nowhere.

pages.title: Notice when searching keeps going
body: Give one harmless chapter, task, piece of music, or hobby ten minutes without unrelated feeds. Make a tally when you want to switch, then return if continuing still makes sense.
Record the tally and one observation. Add a short reminder for the next browsing urge: notice the wish for another option, close the content, and begin your first response.
pages.done: The short practice and reminder are recorded. A tally of zero is fine.

pages.title: Lesson complete.
pages.body: Your answers are saved to the log. One thing left today — the task.

title: Try movement, breathing, or another room

pages.text: No man can step into the same river twice.

pages.title: A response that fits
body: When you feel restless, tense, or worn out, choose a response for that feeling. There isn’t one exercise that suits every difficult evening.
If you’re hungry, food is the obvious beginning. If you’ve been sitting all day, a little movement may fit.
If you’re exhausted, preparing for sleep may help more than another task. If you’re upset about something specific, you may need a pause now and a conversation later.

pages.title: Something to do next
body: A shower, a short walk, stretching, or making a drink can help you interrupt browsing. Choose whichever is accessible and comfortable.
These activities aren’t switches that reliably reset your nervous system or remove desire. Their role is to give you a concrete action between closing the content and returning to the day.
Suppose you feel agitated after work. A long workout might be available, but it might also postpone dinner and bedtime. Try a short walk and food first if those fit better.
You can decide about exercise afterwards. Making the response harder than the problem demands can keep you from beginning.

pages.title: Keep it simple
body: Close the triggering material before using an app or timer. If opening a tool sends you straight back into a feed, use a paper note, an ordinary clock, or no timer. The tool should help the action happen.
Try one response today. If you’re not dealing with an urge, practise its steps without looking for a feeling to fix.
Record whether it was easy to begin. After actual use during an urge, record whether it helped you stop and move on.
Keep one alternative for times the first response doesn’t fit. Going out may be unsafe at night; showering may be unavailable.
A smaller indoor action can still give you a beginning. If these steps repeatedly don’t help with control, add qualified support rather than keep making the same promise stronger.

pages.text: Nothing is permanent except change.

pages.title: Try movement, breathing, or another room
body: Try three minutes of gentle movement, comfortable breathing, or a change of room. Stay within your physical limits and breathe normally if a set rhythm feels uncomfortable.
Describe tension or restlessness before and after, in words or from zero to ten. Record whether you’d use the option again. Stop if it’s uncomfortable.
pages.done: You’ve tried one option and recorded what happened. The feeling doesn’t have to decrease.

pages.title: Lesson complete.
pages.body: One thing left today — the task.

pages.text: Habit is a second nature.

pages.title: Where the habit begins
body: Habits often begin before the moment you call a choice. You finish work, sit in the same chair, open the same account, and only then notice that you’re searching for porn.
Look at that beginning. Which part can you recognise soon enough to act on? Finishing dinner or opening a particular feed may be a better reminder than waiting for an intense urge.
You can put the phone away at that point without first proving you’re about to lose control.

pages.title: Review the changes
body: Review what you changed on Days 22 and 24. Did you move the device, prepare food, or end browsing earlier? What happened on the nights you tried it?
If the situation didn’t happen, say so and check after it does. An unused plan hasn’t failed or succeeded yet.
Keep the comparison modest. One easier night doesn’t prove what caused it.
One difficult night doesn’t show that preparation is worthless. Look for a detail you can repeat or a practical obstacle you can remove.
For example, the phone stayed out of bed on three nights but came back on the night you needed an alarm.
The next change could be an alarm solution, rather than a new argument about discipline. If the device must remain close, decide how to keep its needed functions without resuming the feed.

pages.title: One cue, one response
body: Write one clear cue and response in your plan. You can reuse the sentence from Day 23. Try the steps once so you’re sure they fit your space, then leave them ready for the next time.
You’re building a way to act earlier, not a way to guarantee you’ll never feel tempted. When you notice late, the next step still counts: close the content and begin what follows.
The point of knowing the habit is to make the next decision easier, wherever you catch it.

pages.prompt: What is the earliest step you notice before watching?

options.t: Taking the device to the place where I usually watch
Opening a particular feed or account
Starting sexual searches
Noticing the urge after searching has begun
Another step
I don’t know yet

pages.lead: Put the first response beside the step you actually notice.
body: Catching it later still leaves a chance to stop. If you don’t know yet, observe without seeking a trigger.

pages.text: First we make our habits, then our habits make us.

pages.title: Act earlier in the habit
body: Review the cue change from Day 22 and care adjustment from Day 24. What did you try, and what happened? If you haven’t used either, check the setup and keep the review for after use.
Name the earliest step you can recognise in the browsing habit. Keep a response that helped, or change one step if it didn’t. Practise the beginning without seeking a trigger.
pages.done: The two reviews are recorded or kept for later, and the early response is confirmed or changed.
